title: Frozen and immutable collections (read-only snapshots)
hook: Some data is loaded once at startup and read millions of times — feature flags, route tables, tenant allow-lists. Mutable Dictionary works, but FrozenDictionary and ImmutableDictionary are built for that read-heavy, share-across-threads shape.

blocks.text: System.Collections.Immutable ships types like ImmutableArray<T>, ImmutableList<T>, and ImmutableDictionary<TKey, TValue>. Every "mutation" returns a new copy; the old snapshot stays safe for readers. System.Collections.Frozen (introduced in .NET 8) adds FrozenDictionary<TKey, TValue> and FrozenSet<T> — read-only collections optimized at build time for faster lookups than a regular Dictionary. You build them once from a mutable source, then share the frozen result across all request handlers without locks.

entries.plainDefinition: A read-only hash map from System.Collections.Immutable. Add/Remove return a new dictionary; the original is unchanged.
A read-only dictionary built with ToFrozenDictionary() that trades build-time work for faster runtime lookups.
A struct wrapper around an array that cannot be mutated through the wrapper. Zero-copy when passed by value.
Immutable collections reuse unchanged internal nodes when you create a new version, so small edits do not copy the entire tree.
entries.example: dict2 = dict1.Add("key", 1) shares most nodes with dict1.

blocks.text: A Lambda or ASP.NET Core app that loads tenant feature flags from Redis at cold start can freeze them into a FrozenDictionary and never touch a lock on the hot path. ImmutableDictionary is the right choice when you need occasional updates that produce a new snapshot — configuration reload events, for example. Neither replaces Redis for cross-process sharing; both are in-process, read-only views. Picking a mutable Dictionary and wrapping every read in lock() is the slower, bug-prone alternative.

blocks.title: Build once, read many
blocks.body: FrozenDictionary is for static lookup tables loaded at startup. ImmutableDictionary is for snapshots that occasionally get a new version. Mutable Dictionary is for per-request scratch maps.

sections.heading: How frozen and immutable collections work

items.title: Load mutable data
items.body: Dictionary<string, bool> raw = await LoadFlagsFromRedis(); — normal mutable collection during startup I/O.

items.title: Freeze or make immutable
items.body: FrozenDictionary for max lookup speed on a fixed set. ImmutableDictionary when you expect versioned updates via Add/Remove that return new copies.

items.title: Share across threads
items.body: No locks on reads — the collection cannot change. Safe to store in a static field or inject as a singleton.

items.title: Never mutate after freeze
items.body: FrozenDictionary and ImmutableDictionary throw on Add/Remove. If you need writes, use a new mutable Dictionary and re-freeze.

diagram.title: Read-only collection pipeline
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[Redis / config file] --> B[Dictionary mutable]
  B --> C{Read pattern?}
  C -->|Static lookup table| D[FrozenDictionary]
  C -->|Occasional new version| E[ImmutableDictionary]
  D --> F[Shared across handlers no lock]
  E --> F

snippet.label: FrozenDictionary at startup
snippet.explanation: Load once, freeze with the right comparer, share forever. ToFrozenDictionary does extra work at build time to make TryGetValue faster than a regular Dictionary.

snippet.label: ImmutableDictionary versioned update
snippet.explanation: Each Add/SetItem returns a new dictionary. Readers with v1 see a stable snapshot even after v2 is published. Structural sharing keeps small updates cheap.

snippet.label: ImmutableArray for zero-copy sharing
snippet.explanation: ImmutableArray<T> is a struct wrapping an array. It is ideal for small, fixed allow-lists passed through many method calls without defensive copying.

snippet.label: Failure mode: mutating after freeze
snippet.explanation: Frozen collections are truly read-only. On a config reload event, build a new FrozenDictionary and swap the reference atomically — do not try to patch in place.

blocks.title: Read-only collections across runtimes
rows: Object.freeze is shallow; arrays still mutable at runtime
No built-in frozen Map; use a plain Map or Object
Safe to share read-only snapshots across threads
readonly T[] is compile-time only; erased at run time

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using FrozenDictionary for data that changes every request — the build cost dominates. Assuming ImmutableList is as fast as List<T> for hot loops — it allocates new nodes on every Add. Confusing in-process frozen flags with Redis — FrozenDictionary does not sync across Lambda instances.

blocks.text: FrozenDictionary uses a perfect-hash or minimal-perfect-hash style layout when the key set is known at build time, so TryGetValue avoids the chaining and resize logic of Dictionary<TKey,TValue>. Immutable collections use AVL or hash-array mapped trie structures with structural sharing — an Add on a 10,000-entry ImmutableDictionary does not copy all 10,000 nodes. How to prove it in production: BenchmarkDotNet comparing TryGetValue on Dictionary vs FrozenDictionary with your real key distribution; dotnet-counters to confirm no gen-0 churn from per-request Dictionary allocations after switching to a frozen singleton.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Shared read-only config read millions of times
Startup config, route tables, static lookups
Keys change per request or mid-flight
Hot loops with thousands of Adds per second
Small fixed allow-lists passed by value
Rare writes, many readers, no rebuild
High-contention hot path — prefer immutable swap

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "I'd use ConcurrentDictionary for read-only feature flags" — ConcurrentDictionary is for concurrent writes, not read-only snapshots; it pays synchronization overhead you do not need. Strong answer: load Dictionary at startup, ToFrozenDictionary, inject as singleton, swap atomically on config reload.

interviewTakeaways: FrozenDictionary and ImmutableDictionary are read-only in-process snapshots — not a Redis replacement.
FrozenDictionary trades build-time work for faster TryGetValue; use for static lookup tables loaded at startup.
On config reload, build a new frozen snapshot and swap the reference — never mutate in place.

60s: Load flags into Dictionary, ToFrozenDictionary with the right comparer, share as singleton. ImmutableDictionary when you need versioned Add that returns a new snapshot. Neither crosses process boundaries.
Follow-up: how does FrozenDictionary achieve faster lookups than Dictionary? (perfect/minimal hashing at build time)
commonPitfalls: Saying ConcurrentDictionary is the answer for read-only flags — wrong tool; it pays write-lock overhead you never use.
Strong answer: FrozenDictionary at startup for static lookups; ImmutableDictionary when updates produce new versions; swap reference on reload.
Using FrozenDictionary for per-request data — build cost per request destroys the benefit.
Assuming ImmutableList performs like List<T> in a tight Add loop — each Add allocates new nodes.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Object.freeze is shallow and does not stop array mutation. C# FrozenDictionary is a deep read-only guarantee with optimized lookup — no JS built-in equivalent.
TypeScript readonly is erased at run time — a readonly string[] is still a mutable JS array. C# ImmutableArray and FrozenDictionary enforce immutability in the CLR.
